episode.episode: Philips Hue: The smart home’s light bulb moment
episode.showDescription: Version History is a show about the best gadgets ever. And the worst ones. And the ones that might have changed the world, if they ever actually shipped. Every week, your favorite people from The Verge and beyond hang out to tell and debate the story of a gadget, app, website, or any other tech product, and try to determine the item’s true legacy. Because not every product is a hit, but every product has a story. And the ones that really matter aren’t always the ones you think. From the Verge and the Vox Media Podcast Network.
episode.episodeDescription: The humble light bulb might be the ultimate success story in the smart home. Our connected, adaptable homes are supposed to be customizable, connected to everything, and incredibly easy to use, and nothing has made that work quite like Philips Hue lights. In this episode, The Verge's David Pierce and Jennifer Pattison Tuohy are joined by smart home journalist and expert Richard Gunther to tell the Hue's story. We trace the product's history from its origins in the smartphone revolution, try to figure out how Philips managed to turn a staggeringly expensive lightbulb into a must-have gadget, and look at whether there's even more invention left in the future of lighting. We’re also on video! Check us out on YouTube. Subscribe to The Verge for unlimited access to theverge.com, subscriber-exclusive newsletters, and our ad-free podcast feed. We love hearing from you! transcript_window.text: And it was a sleek, beautiful bulb with this like silver bottom and then the kind of ice cream cone top.
But the original prototypes that they took, that they developed and were sharing with people before they launched, had those big fins and they did not look nice.
They looked like cheap plastic.
And the really interesting thing technology -wise that George shared with me when I talked to him about this is he said they weren't originally looking to develop a colored light bulb.
They were originally looking for tone.
So the warm white to the cool white tone, tunable lighting.
was the kind of that was the thing that had a use case already.
But in order to do that, they had to use very special LEDs.
I think at the time when we were making this, it was just barely possible to make a color changing light bulb in a light bulb form factor.
So the first light bulb we made was was not a 60 watt equivalent.
It was like 45 watts equivalent.
equivalent, didn't do saturated colors.
We had to use automotive grade electronics inside it because parts of it got up to 125 Celsius.
So it was just barely possible.
And the way we made it just possible was by using a lime green LED, which is the most efficient type of LED, in order to boost the amount of white light that we could generate.
And that meant actually kind of colors Side note, when George talks about it, he calls them lead lighting, which is a lot easier to say.
I like that.
Lead lighting.
Interesting.
I have never heard it called that.
I've either.
And then they realized, okay, color shades, adding color gives this a whole different value.
It's a different product and another value proposition.
So, yeah, it was a real – and then they used another company within Philips, Color Kinetics, to help develop the light, the color light.
And Color Kinetics is still around, and it's the company that, like, lights up the Empire State Building and does stuff like that.
Very cool company and a very smart acquisition on Philips' part.
